thread.title: Two Russell Platt works take the stage this week in Wisconsin
thread.title_full: Two Russell Platt works take the stage this week in Wisconsin

author: Blair School of Music
title: Two Russell Platt works take the stage this week in Wisconsin
text:
Two compositions by Blair School of Music professor Russell Platt will be heard on consecutive nights in Wisconsin this week, including a recent work beginning a series of performances around the country and a decades-old concerto given new life through Platt’s collaboration with Blair colleague Mariam Adam.
Russell Platt On Friday, Oct. 16, the University of Wisconsin–La Crosse Wind Ensemble will perform Platt’s Arizona Echoes: Symphonia for Concert Band , the first in a series of performances of the work by university ensembles around the country since its world premiere at Vanderbilt in April 2025. The following evening, Adam, professor of clarinet at Blair, will perform Platt’s Clarinet Concerto with the La Crosse Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Platt’s brother, Alexander Platt.
The back-to-back performances are a coincidence, Platt said, but one that highlights Wisconsin’s strong musical culture.
The University of Wisconsin-La Crosse Wind Symphony performs Russell Platt’s Arizona Echoes: Symphonia for Concert Band on Oct. 16, 2026. Arizona Echoes was Platt’s first composition for concert band, a format he embraced at the encouragement of Vanderbilt Wind Symphony conductor Thomas Verrier. Verrier served as lead commissioner for the project and helped Platt navigate the particular demands of writing for a large wind ensemble.
Inspired by a visit to the USS Arizona Memorial at Pearl Harbor, the work received its world premiere at Vanderbilt on April 5, 2025. Platt subsequently made revisions to the score with Verrier’s guidance.
“I’d never written a band piece before,” Platt said. “So, I decided to deep dive and do a full symphony for a full concert band.”
Platt will speak with the audience and introduce Arizona Echoes before the Wind Ensemble performs the work under the direction of Martin I. Gaines.
The work was commissioned through a consortium of university band programs, with Vanderbilt serving as the lead institution. Following the UW–La Crosse performance, Arizona Echoes will travel to Florida Atlantic University for a Dec. 2 performance conducted by Kyle Prescott, with additional university performances expected in the spring.
Saturday’s concert turns to a work with a much longer history.
Platt began sketching his Clarinet Concerto in 2000 while living in Minnesota. After moving to New York to join the staff of The New Yorker , the events of Sept. 11, 2001, profoundly affected the work, which he completed in 2003.
“The experience of living through 9/11 and being in the 9/11 city definitely clouded the piece,” Platt said. “It’s a tragic kind of work, and it’s not unaffirmative, but it has a tragic scope.”
After joining the Blair faculty, Platt’s work with Adam and other Blair colleagues inspired him to revisit the concerto more than two decades later. He completely reorchestrated the score, replacing its original symphonic strings and large percussion complement with chamber orchestra, percussion and piano, giving the new version what Platt describes as a more distinctly American sound.
Adam premiered the reorchestrated concerto with the Manhattan Chamber Players in Woodstock, New York, in summer 2025. Saturday’s La Crosse Symphony performance marks its return with a larger ensemble.
Platt welcomes the Wisconsin programs as a meaningful convergence: two works from different periods of his career reaching new audiences on consecutive nights, each carrying connections to his colleagues and work at Blair. Together, the performances offer a fitting snapshot of a compositional career that continues to evolve, while giving new life to music written across the years.
